WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he slipped away from Air Force One after a trip last month in Turkey because the Secret Service and military wanted him on a “different plane” due to a threat that he insisted didn't scare him. Log in here » WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he slipped away from Air Force One after a trip last month in Turkey because the Secret Service and military wanted him on a “different plane” due to a threat that he insisted didn’t scare him. Trump downplayed the extraordinary nature of the subterfuge involved in his flight, which saw him stow away in an airport catering container to sneak onto another plane while Air Force One was sent into the sky, essentially as a decoy. He also downplayed the risk to the people — White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters — he left on the plane. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, different plane,” Trump told reporters after returning from an event in Ohio, saying he had little choice in the matter. “I guess there was a threat out there. I didn’t really ask too much about it,” he said. “I get a lot of threats.” His comments confirmed a report that first appeared in The Washington Post saying that Trump, following a NATO summit last month, was spirited onto a different plane because of a credible threat from Iran. The action was kept secret for weeks, until the newspaper’s story. “I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump said Tuesday, who did not provide many details about the action. But he said the incident did not scare him. “I don’t worry about anything, to be honest,” Trump said. “Whatever it is. You know my attitude? Whatever!” Presidents often take secret trips — but not like this Commanders in chief have sometimes kept overseas trips covert for security reasons, with schedules and logistics kept classified until after for safety reasons. But the fact that Trump’s whereabouts were concealed at the time and for weeks afterward is believed to be unprecedented. “We have absolutely seen the president fly on unmarked or decoy planes before, into Iraq, Afghanistan, other war-zone-like places,” said Garrett M. Graff, author of “Raven Rock: The Story of the U.S. Government’s Secret Plan to Save Itself — While the Rest of Us Die.” “But this was an ongoing secret that I don’t think we’ve ever seen before.” After hiding in the catering vehicle and being moved to the other plane, Trump stopped in Britain, sneaked back aboard the presidential plane undetected, and even later scoffed when asked about potential danger. “If I go, you go. Right?” he told reporters then — gliding past the fact that if the plane had been shot down, the president wouldn’t have been aboard. Many details about what happened remain unknown The president’s flight out of Turkey made headlines at the time because he had arrived aboard a luxury jet gifted by Qatar, which was not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets. Trump ended up traveling in a smaller government aircraft from Turkey to the United Kingdom, only to secretly reboard the decoy jet, then descend from it and climb back aboard the Qatari plane. Presidents have regularly tested the confines of their office, pushing their security advisers to visit war zones as a show of American presence and their own leadership. Usually, this happens in the form of trips that aren’t announced until the president is deemed to be out of harm’s way. What’s different this time is that Trump was covertly separated from the rest of his travelers — including the press pool meant to provide independent coverage of the president and his actions — and, instead of informing the public about what occurred once the risk had passed, the White House still hasn’t fully revealed what took place. Graff said the presence of the White House press corps is as much about protecting “the presidency and democracy” as it is about covering the story. “This shows that the White House just fundamentally doesn’t understand how important that role is,” he said. Officials have gone to great lengths to keep presidents safe on covert trips before In 2023, a motorcade pulled away from the White House around 3:30 a.m. on a Sunday, and President Joe Biden later boarded an Air Force C-32, a modified Boeing 757 normally used for domestic trips to smaller airports, and flew to Poland. Biden then took a secret, 10-hour overnight train ride to Kyiv meant to show solidarity with Ukraine after Russia’s invasion. A press pool at the White House had been expecting a quiet Sunday for Biden in Washington. However, two journalists went to Ukraine with him and documented the trip, capturing images of Biden and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walking together. In Trump’s first term, he made a secret Thanksgiving trip to Afghanistan in 2019, when officials kept a separate press pool and decoy plane in Florida to maintain the illusion that the president was spending the holiday at his Mar-a-Lago estate. Instead, Trump and another group of reporters flew to the U.S. military base at Bagram, where the president served turkey to troops, gave a speech and met with Afghanistan’s then-president, Ashraf Ghani, while journalists documented what was occurring. When President George W. Bush made his first trip to Iraq in 2003, news was not released until he was in the air on the way back to the United States. President Barack Obama made a furtive nighttime visit to Afghanistan in 2010, when he was meant to be spending the weekend at Camp David. Other risky trips featured presidential misdirection President Bill Clinton went secretly from India to Pakistan in 2000, attempting to calm tensions in the disputed Kashmir region. He was seen talking with officials in front of a military plane that he appeared to board. Instead, Clinton ducked around the front of the aircraft to another jet parked nearby. Both planes took off for Islamabad, as did a third jet painted with the familiar baby blue markings of Air Force One. Joe Lockhart, a White House press secretary for Clinton, noted that reporters knew the president was on one of the planes, “but not which one.” He said he and other officials had briefed the press pool ahead of time and “although they didn’t know all the details, it was made clear” that Clinton “was not going to travel on the plane they were on. “There was no attempt to hide anything, much less lie about it later,” Lockhart wrote on social media. Bush was visiting an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, during the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, and, after all commercial air traffic was grounded, officials wanted to move him to an undisclosed location. The full White House traveling press pool flew with Bush from Florida to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, where officials reduced the number of reporters and staff on the plane. Bush and the smaller traveling party next flew to Nebraska’s Offutt Air Force Base before eventually returning to Washington. Bush’s location remained secret throughout the day. However, the White House did not suggest that the president was somewhere he was not — unlike when Trump was whisked out of Turkey. “You can imagine the different ways that this could have gone wrong, where, for a period of time, no one would have been able to independently corroborate the status of the U.S. president, or who was in charge of the U.S. government,” Graff said. “And that’s an incredibly dangerous moment for the world.” Advertisement Advertise With Us Advertisement Advertise With Us Tweet Share Print Email Read Later Report Error Submit a Tip Advertisement Learn more about Brandon Sun Advertising solutions World LOAD WORLD ARTICLES

Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An Oxfam shop in London. Oxfam’s retail head said the shift had been ‘challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector’. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian Charities UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted Harry Cockburn Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.10 EDT First published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat. According to unpublished accounts seen by the Financial Times , Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year. The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores after they made a loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops. But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData. The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves. View image in fullscreen The British Heart Foundation, which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Alongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing. “It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times. Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops. In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shops plunged from £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025. The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March. The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes. Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World, described the sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases. “Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said. Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.” View image in fullscreen Oxfam’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock But he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things. “The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships. “The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.” Bafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest tickets Read more Osterley instead suggested the November 2024 budget had had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy. Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future. “The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model. He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.” Explore more on these topics Charities Retail industry Oxfam Voluntary sector news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Naomi Campbell wins legal challenge over charity trustee ban Online marketplaces report surge in sales of secondhand goods Secondhand style strides forward in Oxfam’s London fashion week show Charity threatens legal action over two-year NHS wait for ADHD and autism assessments Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card Cheap, cool and kind to nature: how secondhand became UK fashion’s main attraction Parents shocked after children’s paper hedgehogs found to contain pages from explicit novel Resale therapy: charities reinvent former Topshop to take on Depop and eBay Love Island and eBay renew deal after ‘pre-loved’ clothing boost British Heart Foundation to close 150 charity shops as costs rise Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://hotnews.ro/alegeri-franta-sondaj.text: Liderul de extremă stânga din Franța nu a fost afectat de atacurile guvernului, pe fondul protestelor din ultimele săptămâni, și își consolidează locul doi în vederea alegerilor prezidențiale din primăvara anului viitor, potrivit unui nou sondaj Harris Interactive. Marine Le Pen și Jean-Luc Mélenchon continuă să ocupe primele locuri în preferințele francezilor înaintea alegerilor prezidențiale din aprilie-mai 2027, cu un avantaj clar pentru Le Pen. Candidata grupării de extrema dreaptă Adunarea Națională (RN) este creditată cu 34–36% din intențiile de vot în primul tur de scrutin, arată sondajul Harris Interactive publicat luni. Le Pen îl devansează cu mult pe candidatul stângii radicale, care ar aduna între 18 și 19%. În schimb, primarul orașului Le Havre, Édouard Philippe, care la un moment dat se afla la egalitate cu Jean-Luc Mélenchon în cursa pentru calificarea în turul al doilea, este acum cu mult în urma acestuia. Cu 11-14% din voturi, el se află acum la o distanță de cinci până la șapte puncte față de Mélenchon. Și candidatul social-democrat Raphaël Glucksmann este în ușoară scădere, cu 11-13% din intențiile de vot. Poziția lui Mélenchon în sondaje sugerează că acesta nu a fost afectat de protestele din ultimele săptămâni și de atacurile pe această temă lansate asupra sa de guvern și de candidații de dreapta și de extrema dreaptă. Partidul său, Franța Nesupusă (LFI), a prevăzut în programul său oficial, publicat vineri, ieșirea țării din NATO. „Retragerea imediată din comandamentul integrat al NATO și, ulterior, în etape, din organizația însăși. Respingerea contribuției cerute de Statele Unite, reprezentând 5% din PIB, destinată cheltuielilor de apărare”, se arată în programul de 222 de pagini al LFI. Franța condusă de Mélenchon ar continua să ofere asistență țărilor din Uniunea Europeană în conformitate cu tratatele UE, se mai precizează în document. Zilele trecute, Mélenchon a fost acuzat de guvernul francez că s-a transformat „în purtătorul de cuvânt al Kremlinului” după ce a afirmat că este necesară o consultare a populației din Donbas – regiunea din estul Ucrainei ocupată în mare parte de ruși – cu privire la viitorul acesteia. Una dintre informațiile noului sondaj al institutului Harris este scăderea lui Édouard Philippe, unul dintre candidații cu șanse în fața lui Marine le Pen. Presat de numeroși actori de centru și dreapta să accepte ideea unor alegeri primare, Philippe a reușit în același timp să se distanțeze de majoritatea concurenților săi, dar pare să se confunte cu o provocare, în persoana lui David Lisnard, conservator, lider al partidului Nouvelle Énergie și primar al orașului Cannes. Lisnard, care a înregistrat o evoluție pozitivă în sondaje în ultimele săptămâni, este creditat cu 9% din voturi, la trei puncte în urma lui Philippe (12%) atunci când acesta din urmă este candidat, și la egalitate cu Gabriel Attal (Renaissance) atunci când acesta reprezintă tabăra macronistă (în ambele cazuri, Bruno Retailleau fiind, de asemenea, candidat). În turul al doilea, Marine Le Pen ar câștiga detașat, indiferent de adversar, dar victoria sa ar fi cea mai categorică în fața lui Jean-Luc Mélenchon (68% din voturi față de 32%). În fața lui Édouard Philippe, candidata de extremă dreaptă ar obține 58% din voturi și în fața lui Raphaël Glucksmann ar aduna 60%. Acest sondaj a fost realizat online în perioada 3-5 noiembrie pe un eșantion de 2.101 de persoane înscrise pe listele electorale, reprezentativ pentru populația franceză cu vârsta de peste 18 ani.
